examples.solution_text:
Multiply each outcome by its probability.
$\begin{array}{c|cccc}x&-2&0&3&5\\\hline P(X=x)&0.2&0.1&0.4&0.3\\xP(X=x)&-0.4&0&1.2&1.5\end{array}$
$\begin{align*}E(X)&=-0.4+0+1.2+1.5\\&=2.3\end{align*}$

examples.question_text: A distribution is given by $\left(0,\frac14\right)$, $\left(2,\frac12\right)$ and $\left(4,\frac14\right)$. Find $E(X)$.
examples.solution_text:
Each pair gives an outcome and its probability.
$\begin{array}{c|ccc}x&0&2&4\\[6pt]\hline P(X=x)&\frac14&\frac12&\frac14\\[6pt]xP(X=x)&0&1&1\end{array}$
$\begin{align*}E(X)&=0+1+1\\&=2\end{align*}$

examples.question_text: A random variable has $P(x)=\frac{x+1}{12}$ for $x\in\{1,3,5\}$. Find $E(X)$ in exact form.
examples.solution_text:
Substitute each outcome into the probability rule, then calculate the products.
$\begin{array}{c|ccc}x&1&3&5\\[6pt]\hline P(x)&\frac{2}{12}&\frac{4}{12}&\frac{6}{12}\\[6pt]xP(x)&\frac{2}{12}&\frac{12}{12}&\frac{30}{12}\end{array}$
$\begin{align*}E(X)&=\frac{2+12+30}{12}\\&=\frac{44}{12}\\&=\frac{11}{3}\end{align*}$

examples.question_text: A random variable has $P(x)=k(x+2)$ for $x\in\{0,1,2\}$. Find $k$ and $E(X)$.

A bag contains four white marbles and two black marbles. Two marbles are selected at random without replacement. Let $X$ be the number of black marbles selected. Construct the probability distribution and find $E(X)$.
examples.solution_text:
For exactly one black marble, include both drawing orders.
$\begin{align*}P(X=0)&=\frac46\times\frac35\\&=\frac25\end{align*}$
$\begin{align*}P(X=1)&=\frac26\times\frac45+\frac46\times\frac25\\&=\frac{8}{15}\end{align*}$
$\begin{align*}P(X=2)&=\frac26\times\frac15\\&=\frac{1}{15}\end{align*}$
$\begin{array}{c|ccc}x&0&1&2\\[6pt]\hline P(X=x)&\frac25&\frac{8}{15}&\frac{1}{15}\\[6pt]xP(X=x)&0&\frac{8}{15}&\frac{2}{15}\end{array}$
$\begin{align*}E(X)&=0+\frac{8}{15}+\frac{2}{15}\\&=\frac23\end{align*}$
Over many repeats, the average number of black marbles selected is $\frac23$ per pair.

examples.question_text:
The distribution below has $E(X)=3.4$. Find $p$ and $q$ by setting up two equations.
$\begin{array}{c|ccc}x&1&3&5\\\hline P(X=x)&p&0.4&q\end{array}$
examples.solution_text:
Use the probability total and the expected value.
$\begin{align*}p+0.4+q&=1\\p+q&=0.6\end{align*}$
$\begin{align*}1p+3(0.4)+5q&=3.4\\p+5q&=2.2\end{align*}$
Substitute $p=0.6-q$ into the second equation.
$\begin{align*}0.6-q+5q&=2.2\\4q&=1.6\\q&=0.4\end{align*}$
$\begin{align*}p&=0.6-0.4\\&=0.2\end{align*}$

examples.question_text: Two players have expected numbers of goals per match of $1.7$ and $1.5$. Who scores more goals per match in the long run? Explain why an expected value of $1.7$ is sensible even though goals are counted in whole numbers. Find each player's expected total over $20$ matches and explain whether these totals are guaranteed.
examples.solution_text:
The first player has the greater expected value, so their average number of goals per match is higher over many matches.
An expected value of $1.7$ describes a long-run average. It need not be a possible score in one match.
For the first player, the expected total over $20$ matches is $20(1.7)=34$ goals.
For the second player, the expected total over $20$ matches is $20(1.5)=30$ goals.
These are expected totals, not guaranteed results.
